status_summary: The IAEA found particles of up to 83.7% at Fordow in January 2023 but no accumulation of material above 60%.
Iran made uranium enriched up to 60%, with 440.9 kg as of 13 June 2025; since the strikes the IAEA cannot say how large the stock is, where it is, or whether enrichment has stopped.
US intelligence says the 2025 strikes 'obliterated' the enrichment programme and Iran has made no effort to rebuild it.

US intelligence estimates put the time to enough weapon-grade uranium at about nine months to a year since the June 2025 strikes (anonymous sources); the Energy Secretary said 'a small number of weeks'.
assessed_by: US intelligence (via Reuters); US Department of Energy

status_summary: Iran produced small quantities of uranium metal in 2021, including metal enriched up to 20%, a step the JCPOA prohibited as a key capability for weapons.
Since the 2025 attacks the IAEA has had no access to the conversion and fuel-making plants at Isfahan and cannot assess their status or that of the material in them.
Iran may lack enough experience in producing uranium metal, which for a weapon must be cast and machined into components.
Iran halted its weapon design and weaponization work in fall 2003 and had not restarted it as of mid-2007.
A coordinated programme of work relevant to a nuclear explosive device ran until the end of 2003, with some activities to 2009; it did not go beyond feasibility and scientific studies.
Iran is not currently undertaking the key weapons-development activities needed for a testable device, but is better positioned to produce one if it chooses.
Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and Khamenei had not reauthorized the programme suspended in 2003, though pressure had probably built on him to do so.
Israel's prime minister said Iran had in recent months taken steps 'to weaponise this enriched uranium'.

The 2026 assessment does not address Iran's weapons work; the US is watching whether current or new leaders will authorise a weapons programme. The IAEA had no information in June 2025 of a structured programme to build a weapon (Grossi, 4 March 2026).
assessed_by: ODNI; IAEA Director General (both as reported by CRS)

status_summary: IAEA reports have indicated Iran does not yet have a viable weapon design or a suitable detonation system; the current US timeline for weaponization is unclear (about a year in 2015 and 2022).
The US judged Iran would likely choose missile delivery as its preferred method of delivering a nuclear weapon.
The IAEA verified two workshops named in documents on integrating a payload into a missile, but has had no further information on this since 2011.
Before the 2026 war Iran was pursuing increasingly capable missiles and had space-launch vehicles it could use to develop a military-viable ICBM by 2035 should it decide to.
